patches.old: You don't need to draw literal diagrams on your scratch paper (though some students find this helpful).
patches.new: You don't need to draw literal diagrams on the noteboard booklet the test center gives you (though some students find this helpful).
patches.reason: The MCAT supplies a laminated noteboard booklet and fine-point marker; personal scratch paper is not allowed.

patches.old: If a paragraph seems off-topic, look harder—authors in CARS passages rarely include material that doesn't serve the argument in some way.
patches.new: If a paragraph seems off-topic, look harder—authors in CARS passages rarely include material that serves no purpose. Note, though, that "serving a purpose" is broader than "supporting the thesis": a paragraph may supply background that motivates the inquiry or sets the stakes without acting as a premise in the argument.
patches.reason: As written this conflicted with question 460, whose correct answer is a background paragraph that provides no direct logical support.

visual.title: Claims, evidence, reasoning — and four passage shapes
visual.alt: On the left, three stacked parts of an argument: a claim, the contestable assertion the author wants accepted; evidence, such as data, examples, expert testimony or analogy; and reasoning, the unstated bridge explaining why that evidence supports that claim, with a note that assumption, strengthen and weaken questions all target this implicit layer. On the right, four recurring passage shapes: thesis plus support, problem to solution with its pivot, dialectical moving from position A through a critique to the author's position B, and concession followed by rebuttal. A closing box warns that the author's position sits in the refutation rather than the concession, and that explaining a view at length is not endorsing it.
visual.caption: Find the claim, then ask what must be true for the evidence to reach it.
